events.text: Your first morning as Marquis. A steward you have never met is waiting at the gate with a ledger, a seal box and a list of three counties. Behind him, forty people are kneeling in the frost. You learn later that most of them want something, and the rest want to see what you look like.

choices.text: Ride out and see the three counties yourself

effects.log: Three counties, eleven days, one lame horse. You learn which bridges are lies on the ledger. The steward learns you will check.

choices.text: Remit a year of the fief tax

effects.log: The kneeling crowd goes very quiet, then very loud. The steward looks at the ledger as if it has died in his arms.

choices.text: Hear every petition before breakfast

effects.log: A boundary stone, two widows, a buffalo. By noon you know the fief better than the court that gave it to you.

events.text: The edict is read in the courtyard of your house, and then the yellow register is brought out so you may see your own name in it, one line below the dragon. The ink is still wet. A eunuch blots it with great ceremony. Your cook, who has known you for twenty years, now will not meet your eyes.

choices.text: Bow to the edict, and then to the cook

effects.log: The court officials are scandalised. The cook cries into the soup. It is the best soup of the year.

choices.text: Ask to see the line above yours

effects.log: The eunuch turns pale and closes the register. One line below the dragon is still a line below the dragon.

choices.text: Give a feast for the whole ward (100 taels)

effects.log: Lanterns from your gate to the canal. By morning the ward calls you the Prince of Dumplings. There are worse names. (-100 taels)

events.text: The regent's seal is heavier than it looks. The boy on the dragon throne is seven and has decided to sit perfectly still all morning, as he was told. Only his eyes move. They follow you. When the court bows, it bows to the throne, and then, half a breath later, to you. Everyone notices the half breath.

choices.text: Kneel to the boy first, where all can see

effects.log: The boy stares. The court stares. Then the old ministers bow lower than before. Heaven, they say, notices such things.

choices.text: Take the seat at the throne's right hand

effects.log: Close enough to whisper to the throne. Close enough, the court says, to sit on it. You let them say it.

choices.text: Spend the afternoon reading every pending edict

effects.log: Three hundred edicts. Ninety are lies, forty are traps, one is about a dam that will break in spring. You start with the dam.

events.text: The Mid-Autumn banquet in the palace. Moon cakes, chrysanthemum wine, a pipa player who is very good and very nervous. The wine steward fills every cup from the gold jar, and then fills yours from a small blue one. The wine smells faintly of bitter almonds. Across the hall, nobody is looking at you very hard.

choices.text: Dip your silver hairpin in the cup

effects.log: The silver comes out black. You set the cup down, smile at the moon, and memorise the steward's face.

choices.text: Burn it out with your qi, and pour it away

ok.log: You draw the poison into your fingertips; your meridians catch fire for a breath, and then it is only wine, which you pour out for the moon. Someone across the hall drops a moon cake.

fail.log: The poison is stronger than your pride. You walk out upright and are sick in the plum garden for an hour. (-15 health)

choices.text: Spill it, laughing, and ask for the gold jar

effects.log: A clumsy noble, everyone thinks. The steward pours from the gold jar with shaking hands. You decide not to know why.

events.text: The wine steward is found the next morning in the palace well. The blue jar is gone. A palace maid says, very quietly, that the steward had a new pair of boots last week, very fine ones, and that they came wrapped in cloth from the Grand Secretary's household.

choices.text: Buy the boots from the steward's widow

effects.log: The cobbler's mark is inside the heel. The cobbler remembers the order. The cobbler remembers who paid.

choices.text: Ask the Grand Secretary to tea

effects.log: The Grand Secretary drinks everything you pour first, without hesitating. Either innocent, or very well practised.

choices.text: Let it lie. A dead steward tells nothing

effects.log: You drop it. The court sees you drop it, and decides you are either frightened or patient. You are both.

events.text: A year of quiet. Then the Grand Secretary sends you a gift for your birthday: a blue jar of fine wine, sealed. No letter. Your household stares at it on the table as if it might bite. It is either an apology, a threat, or a joke, and with the Grand Secretary it is usually all three.

choices.text: Bring the jar and the proof before the throne

effects.log: The court gasps in the correct places. The Grand Secretary retires to the provinces for his health. His faction never forgets you.

choices.text: Send back a jar of your own, also sealed

effects.log: Neither jar is ever opened. The two of you are perfectly polite for the rest of your careers. It is a kind of peace.

choices.text: Pour it into the canal in front of the Secretary

effects.log: The fish downstream are fine. The Grand Secretary laughs, for the first time in your hearing. You still do not drink with him.

events.text: A memorial is read at the dawn audience impeaching you. The crime: accepting a box of spring tea from a salt merchant. The author is {npc}, a censor of the seventh rank, in a patched robe, who looks at you without fear and without malice. The tea, in fairness, was very good tea.

choices.text: Admit it in open court and pay the tea's worth

effects.log: The court is baffled. {npc} bows to you, slightly less coldly. The salt merchant stops sending tea.

choices.text: Answer the charge, point by point

ok.log: Gift customs, dates, a ledger. The charge is dismissed. {npc} nods as if this was the right outcome too.

fail.log: You argue well and lose anyway. A month's stipend is docked. {npc} looks almost sorry.

choices.text: Have {npc} posted to the frontier

effects.log: A dusty county at the edge of the steppe. {npc} goes without complaint. The court learns what honesty costs near you.

events.text: {npc} comes to your gate at night, alone, carrying a second memorial. This one impeaches the Chief Eunuch for selling posts in the salt bureau. Every word is true. {npc} asks for your name beside {his}. Everyone who has signed such a thing before has died of something sudden.

choices.text: Sign it

effects.log: Two names on one memorial. The Chief Eunuch is dismissed in a month. You change the guards at your gate the same week.

choices.text: Advise {npc} to wait for a better year

effects.log: {npc} listens, and folds the memorial away, and does not hide that {he} thinks less of you.

choices.text: Warn the Chief Eunuch quietly

effects.log: The Chief Eunuch is very grateful, in silver. {npc} is transferred to a post nobody has heard of.

events.text: Years later {npc} kneels at the Meridian Gate in the rain, sentenced to forty strokes for a memorial that called the throne's new pleasure garden a waste. The rain is cold. The court files past {him} to the audience, looking straight ahead.

choices.text: Kneel beside {npc} in the rain

effects.log: Two officials kneeling in the rain. The strokes are reduced to ten. {npc} never thanks you, and never needs to.

choices.text: Write a memorial of your own for mercy

ok.log: Your memorial is so well made that the throne reads it twice. {npc} is spared, and sent home to recover.

fail.log: Your memorial is read and ignored. The strokes are given. You visit {npc} with ointment every night for a month.

choices.text: Walk past with the others

effects.log: You look straight ahead. Behind you the strokes are counted aloud. You hear every number.

events.text: After the audience the boy emperor, {npc}, climbs down from the throne by {him}self and asks you, very seriously, why your cushion has more tassels than the other ministers'. The eunuchs freeze. {He} is a child. {He} is the Son of Heaven. {He} is waiting for an answer.

choices.text: Cut off your extra tassels, then and there

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud in the throne hall. The eunuchs are horrified. It is the first time you have heard the boy laugh.

choices.text: "Because the Regent carries more."

effects.log: {npc} thinks about this for a long time, and then asks how heavy. You find you do not have a short answer.

choices.text: "Ask your tutors. I am busy."

effects.log: {npc} goes to ask. The tutors give twelve answers, all of them flattering. The boy remembers that you did not.

events.text: {npc} is older now and has two kinds of days: the days you teach the classics, and the days the eunuchs bring crickets in gold cages and kites shaped like dragons. The court is watching which kind of days become more common. So is the boy.

choices.text: Teach the classics yourself, every morning

effects.log: Mencius at dawn. {npc} falls asleep twice and asks one question that keeps you awake all night.

choices.text: Let the eunuchs have the boy's days

effects.log: Crickets, kites, sweets. The boy grows happy, soft, and very easy to sign for. The old ministers say nothing, loudly.

choices.text: Take the boy riding outside the walls

effects.log: {npc} sees a rice field for the first time and asks who owns it. Then who owns the farmer. It is a long ride home.

events.text: At the audience {npc}, taller now and no longer a small child, overrules you. Quietly, correctly, in front of everyone: your flood relief should go to the lower river first, not the upper. {He} is right. The court holds its breath to see what a Regent does when a boy is right.

choices.text: Bow, and say "Your Majesty is right."

effects.log: The court exhales. {npc} goes red to the ears. The rice on the lower river is saved, and so, perhaps, is the boy.

choices.text: Agree, and then go over the figures alone with {him}

effects.log: {He} was right for the wrong reason. Now {he} is right for the right one. That is the whole of teaching.

choices.text: Overrule the child. A Regent rules here

effects.log: The upper river gets the relief. {npc} says nothing. That night the boy copies out the regency laws by candlelight.

events.text: The Chief Eunuch brings you a list. It names everyone who would object if {npc}, now older and still very fond of crickets, were to abdicate for {his} health and live in a comfortable temple. The list is short. Your name is not on it. The eunuch is smiling.

choices.text: Burn the list in front of the eunuch

effects.log: The eunuch stops smiling. You start the classics again the next morning. The boy is behind, but not lost.

choices.text: Keep the list. A Regent should know these things

effects.log: Twelve names. You visit each of them over the next year, one by one, and none of them is on any list again.

choices.text: Have the eunuch arrested for treason

effects.log: The Chief Eunuch is taken in the night. {npc} asks where the eunuch went. You do not have a good answer for a child.

events.text: The Chief Eunuch walks beside you down the long corridor, hands in his sleeves, and mentions that audiences with the throne have become very crowded. A small gift at the inner gate, he says, keeps one's memorials near the top of the pile. He names a sum. He says it as if he were naming the weather.

choices.text: Pay it (60 taels)

effects.log: Your memorials rise to the top of the pile like cream. You feel slightly dirty and very efficient. (-60 taels)

choices.text: Smile and say your memorials can wait

effects.log: They wait. Some of them wait for a year. The Chief Eunuch is perfectly courteous to you, which is worse.

choices.text: Ask him, loudly, to repeat the sum

effects.log: Three ministers turn round. The Chief Eunuch repeats nothing and walks on. You have an enemy who never raises his voice.

events.text: The Empress Dowager invites you to tea in the Pavilion of Lingering Fragrance and talks for an hour about her plum trees. Which bloom early, which sulk, which must be pruned hard before they get ideas. She never says anything else. When you leave, a lady-in-waiting presses a pruning knife into your hands.

choices.text: Prune the Dowager's enemies, as asked

effects.log: A minister of rites is quietly retired that spring. The Dowager sends you plum wine. It is excellent.

choices.text: Return the knife with a branch of blossom

effects.log: She laughs behind her fan, the lady-in-waiting says later. Nobody has refused her so beautifully in years.

choices.text: Take up gardening, and talk only of plums

effects.log: For three years you and the Dowager discuss grafting. You are never asked to prune anything else. You become good at plums.

events.text: The court has split again, as it does every ten years like a bamboo. The Northern faction wants war with the steppe. The Southern faction wants a new canal. Both have invited you to dinner on the same night, at houses on opposite sides of the capital. Your sedan bearers are looking at you expectantly.

choices.text: Dine with the North

effects.log: Mutton, generals, toasts to dead heroes. You come home smelling of war. The Southern faction has already heard.

choices.text: Dine with the South

effects.log: Fish, poets, toasts to rivers. You come home with three new friends and a canal plan. The North has already heard.

choices.text: Eat noodles at home and send both your regrets

effects.log: Both factions are offended and neither can afford to be. For a year everyone courts you. It is exhausting.

events.text: The Board of Rites has been arguing for four months about whether the spring sacrifice robe should be the blue of the sky at dawn or the blue of the sky at noon. Two officials have resigned. One has fainted. It is now your turn to give an opinion, and the whole hall is waiting.

choices.text: Dawn. Beginnings matter

effects.log: The Dawn faction carries you out of the hall in triumph. The Noon faction will not speak to you until autumn.

choices.text: Noon. The sun should see the rite

effects.log: The Noon faction weeps with joy. One old official from the Dawn side sends you a very long poem about betrayal.

choices.text: "The colour of the dyer's best vat."

effects.log: Silence. Then the oldest minister laughs until he cries. The robe is dyed in whatever was in the vat. Heaven seems content.

events.text: Your steward rides in from the fief with the harvest figures and a face like wet paper. The upper county flooded. The lower county did not, and has quietly been selling its rice to the upper county at three times the price. Both counties are yours. Both have written to complain about the other.

choices.text: Fix a fair price across the fief

effects.log: The lower county grumbles and sells. The upper county eats. Next year both of them send you rice cakes, which is suspicious.

choices.text: Open your own granary to the upper county (80 taels)

effects.log: Your granary empties and your name fills. Peasants in the upper county start calling you the Rice Marquis. (-80 taels)

choices.text: Tax the lower county's profits

effects.log: The lower county pays and sulks. The treasury of the fief has never looked healthier. The upper county is still hungry.

events.text: Bandits in the hills of your fief. Your steward wants soldiers. Your magistrate says the bandits are veterans of the last northern war who were never paid, and who still salute when an official passes. One of them sent you a letter. The handwriting is better than the magistrate's.

choices.text: Ride up alone and talk

effects.log: You eat their thin soup and listen to their war. They come down in spring as the fief's militia. They still salute.

choices.text: Pay what the throne never paid (100 taels)

effects.log: A hundred taels, counted out on a rock. The veterans go home. Some cry. All of them remember your name. (-100 taels)

choices.text: Clear the hills by force

ok.log: Old soldiers fight well. You fight better. The survivors are given land in the lower county and watched closely.

fail.log: Veterans know hills. You learn that the hard way. You come back with an arrow scar and nothing else. (-10 health)

events.text: A prince's household, you learn, is three hundred people, of whom two hundred are needed and one hundred are someone's cousin. The kitchen alone spends more in a month than your whole family did in a year. The Head Steward presents the accounts on a scroll so long that two servants hold the ends.

choices.text: Read every line yourself

effects.log: It takes a week. You find a fictitious stable, two dead cooks still drawing wages and a cousin who does not exist. (+100 taels)

choices.text: Dismiss the cousins, gently

effects.log: Ninety cousins go home with a month's wages. Ten weep convincingly enough to stay. The kitchen is suddenly very fast.

choices.text: Keep them all. A prince is a shelter

effects.log: Three hundred people eat because you are a prince. You decide that is not the worst use of a title.

events.text: A swordsman sits outside your gate for three days in the rain without eating and asks to become a retainer of your household. The guards think he is mad. The rain does not seem to touch his sword arm. On the fourth morning a sparrow lands on his scabbard and he does not move.

choices.text: Take him in as your shadow

effects.log: He says nine words in a year. Two assassins are found in the garden the next autumn, very surprised and very dead.

choices.text: Test him first

ok.log: Three exchanges. On the third he stops a hair from your throat and bows. He moves into the gatehouse that night.

fail.log: He disarms you politely and hands your sword back hilt first. You hire him anyway, slightly embarrassed. (-6 health)

choices.text: Feed him and send him on

effects.log: He eats four bowls of rice, bows once, and walks off into the rain. You hear later he guards a temple. Good.

events.text: The throne sends you a gift: a white horse from the western pastures, very tall, very beautiful, and very obviously a test. A prince who rides a white horse through the capital looks like a man who would like a throne. A prince who refuses a gift from the throne looks like something worse.

choices.text: Keep it in the stable and ride a brown one

effects.log: The white horse grows fat and happy. Twice a year you are seen visiting it. The court reads this correctly.

choices.text: Ride it once to the palace to say thank you

effects.log: Every window in the capital opens. The throne receives your thanks with a long, thoughtful look.

choices.text: Give it to the frontier cavalry

effects.log: "Your Majesty's gift belongs where Your Majesty's enemies are." The throne is pleased. The horse is less pleased.

events.text: The dawn audience. You have knelt on the stones of the Meridian Gate since the fourth watch, and it is raining. Old ministers around you are trying not to shiver. The doors stay shut. Somewhere inside, the throne is late, or ill, or simply making a point.

choices.text: Kneel straight until the doors open

effects.log: Four hours. When the doors open you are the only one still kneeling straight. The throne notices. So do your knees.

choices.text: Share your oiled cloak with the old minister

effects.log: Two officials under one cloak. The old man says nothing, but he votes with you for the next ten years.

choices.text: Circulate qi to keep warm, eyes closed

effects.log: Steam rises gently from your shoulders. The ministers nearby edge closer, as people do to a fire.

events.text: A young eunuch bumps into you in the corridor, apologises, and is gone. In your sleeve there is now a folded note in a child's careful hand: the Censorate will search your house tomorrow at the hour of the snake. The boy could not be more than fourteen.

choices.text: Search your own house tonight

effects.log: Under the floor of the guest room: a forged letter in your name to a northern khan. You burn it. The search finds nothing.

choices.text: Find the boy and protect him

effects.log: You buy his contract from the palace and send him to your fief. He becomes a very good clerk, and a better friend.

choices.text: Do nothing. Let them search

effects.log: They find the forged letter, and you have no answer. Only a fortnight of hearings clears you. Next time you will listen.

events.text: You are asked to read papers for the palace examination. The paper at the top of your pile is excellent, and its candidate's name has been neatly pasted over, as the rules require. The paper beneath it is dreadful, and someone has neatly unpasted its name: the nephew of the Duke of Wei.

choices.text: Grade them both exactly as written

effects.log: The nephew fails. The Duke of Wei sends no letter at all, which is a kind of letter. The excellent paper belongs to a fisherman's son.

choices.text: Pass the nephew and pocket the favour

effects.log: The nephew becomes a county magistrate. You hear about his county now and then, never anything good. (+150 taels)

choices.text: Paste the name back on and report it

effects.log: The examiner who unpasted it is dismissed. Nobody can say you did anything except follow the rules. You like that.

events.text: Your seal of office is not in its box. The box is locked. The key is on your belt. Your secretary is pale, the servants are paler, and the next time a document with your seal on it appears, it could say anything at all. There are three days until the next audience.

choices.text: Report it to the throne at once

effects.log: A month's stipend docked and a new seal cut. Two weeks later a forged edict with the old seal fails, because you spoke first.

choices.text: Find it quietly yourself

ok.log: The cat. The cat knocked it into the rafters. You tell nobody this, ever.

fail.log: Three days of searching and nothing. You report it late and are scolded. The cat looks innocent.

choices.text: Have a new one cut in secret

effects.log: The new seal is perfect. Somewhere, the old one is still out there. You sleep less.

events.text: The regency council meets. Five ministers, one Regent, and behind a pale silk screen at the end of the hall, the Empress Dowager, who is not on the council and has never missed a meeting. Every proposal is read aloud. After each one the room waits for the small sound of her fan.

choices.text: Address the screen directly

effects.log: The council gasps. The fan stops. Then, from behind the screen, a dry laugh. From that day the Dowager speaks to you, and only to you.

choices.text: Move the council to a room with no screen

effects.log: The new room is small and cold. The Dowager sends a eunuch to sit in the corner and take notes. It is a draw.

choices.text: Visit her privately before each meeting

effects.log: Tea before every council. By the third month the fan never moves at all, because the two of you have already agreed.

events.text: A frontier general asks for the regent's half of the bronze tiger tally, so his half will match it and the northern army will march. The steppe is raiding. The general is brave, loud, and much loved by his troops. An army that marches can also march back.

choices.text: Give him the tally

effects.log: The army marches north and wins. It comes back south a little too cheerful. You watch the general carefully for years.

choices.text: Ride north with the tally yourself

ok.log: The raids end in one summer. The army cheers the Regent. The general cheers loudest, through his teeth.

fail.log: A season in the saddle, two skirmishes lost and a fever. The general finishes the war. He is very gracious about it. (-8 health)

choices.text: Send a second general to share the command

effects.log: Two generals, two halves, one war. They spend more time watching each other than the steppe. Nobody marches south.

events.text: Someone has written a poem on the wall of the Western Market about you. It is four lines long, very funny, and rhymes your name with a word for a bloated toad. The whole capital is reciting it. The magistrate asks whether you would like the poet found.

choices.text: Find the poet and hire them

effects.log: The poet is a drunk former examiner with a brilliant pen. Your memorials have never read better.

choices.text: Write a better poem in reply, under it

ok.log: Your reply is funnier. The capital laughs with you now. The toad poem is quietly washed off by an admirer.

fail.log: Your reply is earnest and bad. The capital now recites both poems, in that order.

choices.text: Have the wall whitewashed and forget it

effects.log: The wall is white by noon. By evening the poem is on three other walls. Some battles are not worth winning.

events.text: Midwinter. The Hall of Supreme Harmony is unheated by ancient custom, and the ink freezes in the stones. In the middle of a memorial on river taxes, the old Minister of Works sways, and folds to the floor like a dropped robe. The court looks at the throne. The throne looks at the memorial.

choices.text: Go to him, whatever the custom says

effects.log: You hold his wrist and push warm qi into it until his colour comes back. Custom is broken. Nobody dares to mention it.

choices.text: Finish reading his memorial for him

effects.log: You take up the paper and read it through, steady, to the end. The river taxes pass. The old man lives, and is grateful.

choices.text: Propose braziers for the hall

effects.log: The Board of Rites objects for a month. Then the braziers come, and nobody remembers they were ever controversial.

events.text: The first night of the rebellion. The camp is a field of cooking fires that runs to the river. Farmers with spears, sect disciples with swords, a blacksmith who brought his anvil on a cart. Your banner snaps above the command tent. Somewhere in the dark, someone has started a song with your name in it.
events.arc: The First Night Under the Banner

choices.text: Walk the fires and learn their names

effects.log: You stop at forty fires before dawn. By the end of the war, men who never met you swear you knew their fathers.

choices.text: Write the army's laws before you sleep

effects.log: No looting. No burning. Pay for the rice. Eleven laws by candlelight. Heaven, the old scribe says, reads such things.

choices.text: Sit alone by the river and steady your qi

effects.log: The water goes on as if there were no war. By morning so do you. It is the last quiet night for years.

events.text: Three hundred new recruits arrive from the eastern villages. They have spears, hoes, two buffalo, a grandmother who refuses to leave her grandson, and no idea which end of a crossbow to point at the enemy. The drill sergeant looks at them and then at you, like a man drowning politely.

choices.text: Drill them yourself for a month

effects.log: A month of mud and shouting. By the end they can hold a line. The grandmother can hold it better than most.

choices.text: Send the youngest and oldest home

effects.log: Ninety go home, the grandmother taking her grandson by the ear. The rest fight better for knowing you did it.

choices.text: Put them on the supply wagons

effects.log: Farmers know carts, buffalo and rice. Your supply line has never run so well. Armies march on that.

events.text: The quartermaster brings you the sums. Eleven days of rice for twenty thousand mouths. The harvest is a month off. The nearest imperial granary is behind the walls of Qingshui, which is held by a magistrate who has sworn to burn it before he lets you have a grain.

choices.text: Buy rice from the river merchants (300 taels)

effects.log: The merchants charge war prices and smile. The army eats. You write each merchant's name in a small book. (-300 taels)

choices.text: Halve the ration, yours included

effects.log: Thin rice for a month. The soldiers see you eat the same bowl. Nobody deserts. Several write songs about it.

choices.text: Send a letter to the magistrate of Qingshui

ok.log: The magistrate opens the granary and the gate. He was never paid either. The army eats, and gains a magistrate.

fail.log: Your envoy comes back with his ears intact and the letter burned. Qingshui's granary smokes for two days.

events.text: Hejian has walls thirty feet high, a moat full of reeds, and a garrison that empties its chamber pots on your scouts. Your generals want to storm it before the imperial army arrives. Your engineers want three months to dig. Your quartermaster wants to know what everyone will be eating.

choices.text: Storm the walls at dawn

ok.log: Ladders, smoke, and a gate that opens from inside. Hejian falls by noon. The chamber-pot sergeant is the first to surrender.

fail.log: The ladders are too short. The moat is deeper than the scouts said. You pull back at noon, with fewer men and an arrow wound. (-12 health)

choices.text: Dig, and starve them out

effects.log: Three months of tunnels. The garrison eats its horses, then its pride. The gates open to the sound of your shovels.

choices.text: Go round and leave Hejian behind you

effects.log: Hejian is left shouting at an empty field. Three provinces later the city surrenders by letter, embarrassed.

events.text: The imperial army has come at last: sixty thousand under the banners of the old dynasty, drawn up across the plain of red grass. Your army is smaller and hungrier. Your generals wait for your word. On the far side, a lone horseman rides out under a white flag and invites you to single combat with their champion.

choices.text: Ride out and face the champion yourself

ok.log: Three passes. On the third the champion's spear breaks on your blade and the imperial line wavers. Your army roars and charges.

fail.deathCause: killed in single combat before two armies on the plain of red grass
fail.log: The champion's spear finds your ribs. Your generals drag you back. The battle is fought without you, and drawn. (-25 health)

choices.text: Refuse, and hold the line

effects.log: Honour, your generals say, is cheap; men are not. The imperial army charges into your spears and breaks there by dusk.

choices.text: Send your best general to fight in your place

effects.log: Your general wins, barely, and the imperial army loses its nerve. Your general's name is sung louder than yours that night.

events.text: The Yellow River in flood, a mile of brown water, and the imperial cavalry somewhere behind you. The ferrymen say the river cannot be crossed in this season. The ferrymen also say that for enough silver, the river might change its mind.

choices.text: Pay the ferrymen (200 taels)

effects.log: Every boat on the river, for one night. The army crosses by lantern. At dawn the cavalry arrives at an empty bank. (-200 taels)

choices.text: Build rafts from the villages' doors

effects.log: Three villages lose their doors. The army crosses. You send carpenters back after the war, which helps a little.

choices.text: Turn and fight on the near bank

ok.log: The cavalry has never fought with water at its back either. It breaks first. You cross at leisure.

fail.log: A hard day with the river at your back. You cross that night with half the wagons and all the wounded. (-10 health)

events.text: A blind fortune teller is brought to the command tent. In the market of the last town he cast the sticks for your rebellion, and they fell in the shape of the character for dragon. The whole army has heard. Half of them now fight like tigers. The other half want the sticks cast again, just to be sure.

choices.text: Pay him and send him to every camp

effects.log: The sticks fall as a dragon in every camp. You do not ask how. Morale has never been higher. (-30 taels)

choices.text: Tell the army a war is won by rice, not sticks

effects.log: Some are disappointed. More are reassured. The fortune teller nods as if this was also in the sticks.

choices.text: Ask him to cast them for you, alone

effects.log: He casts. He feels the sticks with his fingers for a long time. Then he says only, "Go on." You do not ask any more.

events.text: A great sect sends its disciples down the mountain to join your banner: two hundred swords who can run on rooftops and fight ten soldiers each. Their elder asks only one thing. When you sit on the throne, the murim will be left alone. Forever, in writing.

choices.text: Write it and seal it

effects.log: Two hundred swords join the army. A throne bound by its own promise, the elder says. You hope you remember it.

choices.text: "Forever is a long word for a throne."

effects.log: The elder smiles at last. The disciples come down for years, not forever. It is an honest bargain.

choices.text: Decline. The murim should stay out of this

effects.log: The elder bows and goes back up the mountain. The sect survives the war untouched, and so does its honour.

events.text: Twelve deserters are caught at dawn on the south road with sacks of army rice. They are all from the same village. The youngest is perhaps fifteen. The army's laws, which you wrote, are clear. The whole camp is waiting to see if they are also true.

choices.text: Follow the law

effects.log: The law is followed. No one deserts again for a year. The village never sends another son to your banner.

choices.text: Spare the youngest; flog the rest

effects.log: A rule kept and a mercy given. The camp argues about it all night, which is better than not thinking about it.

choices.text: Ask why they ran, before anything else

effects.log: Their village is starving. You send rice back with them and a promise. They return in a month with forty more.

events.text: Your guards catch the camp cook writing a letter at night. He cannot read, he says, and he was only drawing. The letter lists your troop numbers, very accurately, in a hand far better than any cook's. He is also the best cook the army has ever had.

choices.text: Feed the capital false numbers through him

effects.log: For six months the capital fights an army that does not exist. The cook keeps cooking. He is very nervous, and very good.

choices.text: Hang the spy

effects.log: The capital loses a spy. The army loses its cook. Morale drops more than you would like to admit.

choices.text: Offer him double what the capital pays

effects.log: He accepts with relief. His next letter to the capital is a recipe for pork dumplings. (-50 taels)

events.text: A town opens its gates to you, and its imperial magistrate is brought before you in chains, still wearing his official cap. The townspeople say he was fair. The imperial records say he was fair. He says, very calmly, that he served the throne and will serve no bandit.

choices.text: Release him with an escort to the capital

effects.log: He goes. In the capital he tells everyone you are no bandit. Nobody listens to him, and then, later, everybody does.

choices.text: Keep him to govern the town for you

ok.log: "For the town, not for you," he says. He governs it so well you put three more towns under him.

fail.log: He refuses, politely, every day for a month. In the end you let him go home. He keeps his cap.

choices.text: Hold him for ransom

effects.log: The capital pays for its fair magistrate. A rebel who sells men, the court says now. It is not wrong. (+150 taels)

events.text: Snow comes early. The war stops as wars do in winter, in a ring of frozen tents in the hills. The soldiers huddle and talk about home. Your generals talk about spring. The horses do not talk, but they are eating the thatch off the shelters.

choices.text: Teach the soldiers to read, in the long nights

effects.log: By spring, four hundred soldiers can write their names. Several write home for the first time. It is a better army.

choices.text: Drill them in the snow

effects.log: They curse you every morning and are warm every afternoon. In spring they march faster than the imperial army.

choices.text: Hold a festival on the longest night

effects.log: Pork, wine and a play in which you are played by a very fat sergeant. Nobody deserts that winter. (-40 taels)

events.text: The army has a new marching song. The tune is old; the words are new and about you. In the third verse you kill a tiger with your bare hands. In the fifth verse you are taller than a gate. The soldiers sing it every morning with tremendous feeling, and slightly out of time.

choices.text: Join in on the chorus

effects.log: You sing badly and loudly. The soldiers are delighted. The song gets a sixth verse in which you also sing well.

choices.text: Ask them to cut the tiger verse

effects.log: They cut it. They sing it anyway when they think you are not listening. It is the best verse.

choices.text: Have the scribes write it down

effects.log: The song spreads faster than your army. Towns you have never seen open their gates already singing it.

events.text: Pay day, and the war chest is lighter than the army thinks. The paymaster has done the sums three times. If you pay in full, you can pay twice more. If you pay half, the army will know. If you pay nothing, the army will leave.

choices.text: Pay in full (250 taels)

effects.log: Every soldier is paid to the coin. You count the chest after, alone, for a long time. (-250 taels)

choices.text: Pay half and tell them why

effects.log: Grumbling, and then nodding. Soldiers can forgive a thin purse. They cannot forgive a lie.

choices.text: Pay them from the next city's treasury

effects.log: The next city's treasury is taken and spent in an afternoon. The army is happy. The city is not.

events.text: A drummer boy is found among the new recruits: ten years old, an orphan, beating the march with two sticks and a stolen drum, perfectly in time. He has followed the army for three provinces. He says he is fifteen. He is lying with his whole face.

choices.text: Keep him away from the line, as a messenger

effects.log: He runs messages between the tents and grows two inches. The army adopts him, and he adopts all of it.

choices.text: Send him to a temple to be raised

effects.log: He cries and kicks and goes. Years later a monk with very good timing comes to thank you.

choices.text: Make him the army's drummer

effects.log: The best drummer the army has. He stays at the rear, under the sergeant's eye. Nobody marches out of step again.

events.text: General Zhao and General Kang have quarrelled again, this time with swords drawn in the command tent. Zhao wants to march on the capital now. Kang wants to take the southern granaries first. Each has ten thousand men who would follow him off a cliff, and each is now looking at you.

choices.text: Side with Zhao: march on the capital

effects.log: Kang sheathes his sword very slowly. Zhao's men cheer. Kang's men do not.

choices.text: Side with Kang: take the granaries

effects.log: Zhao spits on the floor of the tent and walks out. Kang bows, too low.

choices.text: Give each half the army and a separate road

effects.log: Two roads, two generals, one war. They will each try to win it first. That may be useful.

events.text: Some time later. A rider brings news from one of your two generals, the one who did not get his way: he has taken a city on his own, without orders, and has sent you its keys with a letter so polite it is almost an insult. His men are calling him by a title that is not quite General any more.

choices.text: Ride to him and embrace him before his troops

effects.log: His men see it. He sees that they saw it. The title quietly goes back to being General.

choices.text: Strip him of command

ok.log: He hands over the seal in a cold rage. His men stay with your banner. He is given a fine house far from any army.

fail.log: He refuses, and takes three thousand men with him into the hills. You will meet them again. (-10 health)

choices.text: Reward him with the city he took

effects.log: A city for a general. He is content, for now. Every other general starts looking at cities.

events.text: Smoke over the village of Lijia. Not imperial troops. Your own vanguard, who were told the village had hidden rice from them. The village had hidden rice from everyone, because it was starving. The survivors stand in the ash and watch your banner ride in.

choices.text: Dismount and walk into the ash

effects.log: You walk the whole village on foot. A woman throws a burnt pot at you. You do not let the guards stop her.

choices.text: Find the officer who gave the order

effects.log: A captain of the vanguard, young and frightened, who says he was obeying your laws. Were they your laws? You go and read them.

choices.text: Ride on. A war has a schedule

effects.log: The army rides past Lijia without slowing. The survivors watch it go. They will tell the story for a hundred years.

events.text: The captain who burned Lijia kneels in front of the army, bound. The village elders are there, and your generals, and the whole vanguard. The elders want his head. The vanguard wants him spared. The army is waiting to see what a rebellion is for.

choices.text: Give the elders what they ask

effects.log: Justice, swift and cold. The elders bow. The vanguard is quiet for a long time, and never burns anything again.

choices.text: Send him to rebuild Lijia with his own hands

effects.log: The captain and his men stay behind with axes. The elders are not satisfied. The new houses are better than the old.

choices.text: Take the blame yourself before the army

effects.log: "The law was mine. So is the ash." The army is stunned. The elders do not forgive you, but they stop cursing.

events.text: Years later, still at war, you pass Lijia again. New roofs. A new well. A temple with a small shrine, and on the shrine, a tablet for the villagers who died the day your banner came. Someone has lit incense. Someone has also, very small, carved your name under theirs.

choices.text: Kneel and light incense of your own

effects.log: The incense burns down. An old man comes and stands beside you. Neither of you says anything. That is enough.

choices.text: Leave silver for the shrine (60 taels)

effects.log: The silver will become rice, a roof, a teacher. It does not become forgiveness. You did not expect it to. (-60 taels)

choices.text: Ask them to remove your name

effects.log: "No," the old man says. "You were there. You should be remembered there." You ride on with that.

events.text: At midnight an imperial general rides into your camp alone, unarmed, and asks for you by name. {npc}, who held the pass at Yanmen against you for two years. {He} says the capital has executed {his} family for {his} failures, and {he} would like to talk about the pass.

choices.text: Take {npc} into your council

effects.log: {npc} draws you the defences of every pass in the north from memory. Your generals hate {him} at once.

choices.text: Hear {npc} out, then send {him} away

effects.log: {npc} rides off into the dark. You never learn whether the story was true. You never stop wondering.

choices.text: Suspect a trap and hold {him} under guard

effects.log: {npc} accepts the guard without a word. Under guard, {he} still draws maps. They are very good maps.

events.text: The pass at Yanmen. {npc}'s maps have been true so far. Tonight {he} offers to lead a hundred men up a goat path {he} alone knows, and open the gate from inside. If {he} is lying, the hundred men will not come back. Your generals are watching your face.

choices.text: Trust {npc}, and send the hundred

ok.log: The gate of Yanmen opens at the fourth watch. {npc} stands in it, bloody and grinning. The north is open.

fail.log: The gate opens onto a trap, but not {npc}'s. {npc} holds it with a spear in {his} side. Half the hundred come home.

choices.text: Go up the goat path with {npc} yourself

effects.log: A night of cliffs and goat dung. The gate opens. {npc} looks at you differently afterwards. So does the army.

choices.text: Refuse, and take the pass the slow way

effects.log: Two more months. {npc} says nothing, and serves, and is never quite trusted. The pass falls anyway.

events.text: An envoy from the capital rides in under a white flag, with a eunuch, a scroll and a box. The terms: lay down your banner, and the throne will grant you a princedom, pardon your army and give you a province to govern. The box holds a jade seal, already cut with your name.

choices.text: Send the envoy back with the box unopened

effects.log: The envoy rides off pale. Your army cheers. The capital now knows you will not be bought.

choices.text: Ask for time to consider

effects.log: The envoy waits a month. You use it to take two cities. The capital learns what you meant by considering.

choices.text: Keep the seal, and the war

effects.log: A fine jade seal, very well cut. It sits on your desk for the rest of the war, reminding everyone that you had a choice.

events.text: The envoy returns. The terms are better this time: two provinces, a princedom, and the old dynasty's daughter for your eldest kin. Your generals are divided. Some are tired. Some are not. Outside, the army has stopped singing and is listening at the tent walls.

choices.text: Refuse again, before the army

effects.log: The army hears it and roars. The envoy goes home for the last time. There will be no more terms; only the end.

choices.text: Demand the capital's granaries as well

effects.log: The envoy sends rice as a sign of good faith while the talks drag on. The talks never end. The rice does. (+200 taels)

choices.text: Send the envoy home with a gift for the throne

effects.log: A gift of tea, a refusal wrapped in silk. The old emperor is said to have laughed. He, at least, sees the end coming.

events.text: The night the rebellion breaks. Your army is a thousand campfires going out one by one across the plain. Your banner is in the river. A handful of guards are still with you, and a horse that keeps stopping to look back. The capital's riders are an hour behind. Perhaps less.

choices.text: Dismiss the guards to save their lives

effects.log: They refuse twice and go the third time. You ride on alone. Most of them live, because you made them go.

choices.text: Ride for the mountains, now

effects.log: Through the night and the next day. By dusk you are in the high passes, and the riders are a rumour behind you.

choices.text: Go back for the wounded

effects.log: You bring out eleven. The riders nearly catch you twice. Eleven families will light incense for you. (-10 health)

events.text: Your face is on the wall of the market, beside a sum of silver large enough to buy the market. The likeness is poor. The nose is wrong. The description below says you are taller than you are, which you find flattering. A noodle seller is looking at the poster, and then at you.

choices.text: Buy a bowl of noodles and leave a large tip

effects.log: The noodle seller looks at the silver, at you, at the poster, and says the nose is wrong. You both agree. (-10 taels)

choices.text: Walk out of town without hurrying

effects.log: You do not hurry. People who hurry are remembered. By evening you are two valleys away.

choices.text: Tear the poster down at night

effects.log: The next morning there are four new ones. One of them has the nose right. Somebody has seen you.

events.text: An old monastery high in the mountains takes you in without a question. You sweep the courtyard, carry water and eat thin rice. The abbot knows exactly who you are. Today a column of imperial riders is winding up the path, and the abbot is calmly making tea.

choices.text: Shave your head and sit among the monks

effects.log: The riders search every cell. They look straight at you and see a monk. The abbot pours them tea. They leave thanking him.

choices.text: Leave by the back path to spare the monks

effects.log: You are gone before they reach the gate. The monastery is untouched. The abbot keeps your broom by the wall.

choices.text: Wait at the gate for them

ok.log: Twelve riders, one gate, one fugitive. The riders go home with sore heads and a story nobody believes.

fail.log: Too many. The monks drag you inside and hide you in the bell tower until the riders tire. (-15 health)

events.text: A bounty hunter finds you at a ferry crossing: a lean woman with a crossbow and a very tired face, who has followed you for three provinces. She does not raise the crossbow. She sits down on the bank and asks whether you would like to talk about the reward first.

choices.text: Ask what she will do with the silver

effects.log: A daughter, a debt, a roof. You listen. In the end she goes home with a story and a letter for a friend who can help.

choices.text: Outrun her on the river

effects.log: Across the ferry ropes and into the reeds. She does not shoot. You think she did not want to.

choices.text: Fight her here and now

ok.log: Short and ugly. She yields, bleeding, and swears to tell the capital you drowned. Perhaps she will.

fail.log: A crossbow bolt through the shoulder before you close. You escape across the river half-drowned. (-12 health)

events.text: In a wine shop at the edge of nowhere, an old man with one arm sets a cup in front of you without being asked. He fought under your banner at the river. He lost the arm there. He does not say any of this. He says only that the wine is on the house, and goes back behind the counter.

choices.text: Sit with him over tea and name the dead

effects.log: Pot after pot of tea, name after name. At dawn he lets you out the back. He never asks why it went wrong. You tell him anyway.

choices.text: Leave everything you have on the counter

effects.log: Not enough for an arm. Enough for a winter. He pretends not to see it until you are gone. (-40 taels)

choices.text: Thank him, leave the cup full, and go before dawn

effects.log: The riders search the wine shop at noon. The old man has never seen anyone. He pours them very bad wine.

events.text: The Great Wall at last, crumbling at this stretch, with a gap where a watchtower fell a hundred years ago. Beyond it, the grass of the steppe to the end of the world. Behind it, everything you were. The guards at the next tower are asleep. They will not be for long.

choices.text: Cross, and do not look back

effects.log: The grass closes behind you. A herding family takes you in. For a while you are only a stranger who is good with horses.

choices.text: Stay on this side. This is still your land

effects.log: You turn back south. Hunted is not the same as finished. You go to find out what you are now.

choices.text: Take a handful of earth with you

effects.log: A pouch of the soil of home, tied at your belt. You cross. Some nights you hold it and do not open it.

events.text: Coronation day. Nine steps up to the throne, each one carved with a dragon, each one longer than it looks. The court kneels in rows that reach the gate. The drums stop. In the silence you can hear the silk of ten thousand sleeves and, somewhere far off, a vendor still selling sesame cakes outside the walls.

choices.text: Climb slowly, looking at every face

effects.log: Ten thousand faces. You remember which ones look away. Most of them will be loyal. You will find out which.

choices.text: Pause on the ninth step and look back

effects.log: You look back down the steps at the life that brought you here. Then you turn and sit. The court lets out its breath.

choices.text: Send the sesame vendor a gold coin

effects.log: The first act of the new reign is a gold coin for a cake seller. The story is all over the capital by dusk. Heaven, they say, approves.

events.text: The Board of Rites presents twelve candidate names for your reign era, each two characters long and each chosen for its meaning, its sound and the number of strokes. The scholars have been arguing for a month. Every coin, every edict and every gravestone for as long as you reign will carry the name you pick.

choices.text: Eternal Peace

effects.log: Eternal Peace it is. The scholars nod. The generals look at each other. Every reign called Peace has had a war; this one will too.

choices.text: Heaven's Favour

effects.log: A bold name. If the harvests are good, it will look like prophecy. If they are not, the people will make jokes about it.

choices.text: Write two characters of your own

ok.log: Your characters are simple and strange and right. The scholars argue for a month about why, which is how they show approval.

fail.log: Your characters have an unlucky stroke count. The scholars quietly add a dot. Nobody ever tells you.

events.text: The first rite in the dynasty's ancestral temple. The tablets of your line are carried in on yellow palanquins, including some ancestors who were pig farmers and one who was, according to the family, a pirate. The Board of Rites has given each of them a new title. The pirate is now a Duke of the Southern Seas.

choices.text: Bow to every tablet, the pirate too

effects.log: Nine bows, one for each. The pirate's tablet gets the deepest. Some families are made by pirates. Yours, apparently, was.

choices.text: Order the true titles carved on the back

effects.log: Front: Duke of the Southern Seas. Back: Pirate. The historians are thrilled. The Board of Rites is not.

choices.text: Feast the capital in the ancestors' names (500 taels)

effects.log: Three days of feasting. The capital drinks to the Duke of the Southern Seas without knowing why. (-500 taels)

events.text: The signs are everywhere this year. Twin ears of grain on one stalk in Henan. A white deer in the imperial park. The Yellow River ran clear for a whole day. The court has written forty-one memorials of congratulation and the Board of Rites has run out of ways to say auspicious.

choices.text: Hold a great sacrifice at the Altar of Heaven

effects.log: Smoke rises straight up into a windless sky. The people say Heaven is listening. For once you rather believe them.

choices.text: Cut the taxes, while Heaven is kind

effects.log: A third off the land tax for a year. The treasury groans. The villages light lanterns in your name.

choices.text: Ignore the signs and inspect the dikes

effects.log: Good years are when you mend the roof. The ministers are puzzled. The dikes hold for years.

events.text: Bad signs. A two-headed calf in Shandong. Hail in summer. The great bell of the capital cracked when it was rung for your birthday. The tea houses have started telling the story of the last dynasty's final emperor, and the storytellers keep pausing at the same places, and the audience keeps laughing.

choices.text: Issue an edict of self-reproach

effects.log: "The fault is the throne's." The edict is read in every square. Some people weep. Some people say it is about time.

choices.text: Ban the storytellers

effects.log: The storytellers stop. Now people tell the stories at home, in whispers, which is worse.

choices.text: Recast the bell yourself, at the foundry

effects.log: The Son of Heaven in a leather apron at the furnace. The new bell rings true. The tea houses tell that story instead.

events.text: The salt monopoly brings in a third of the treasury and makes a few hundred salt merchants richer than princes. The Minister of Revenue proposes raising the salt price again. The people already eat their rice with less salt than their grandparents. Salt smugglers are becoming folk heroes.

choices.text: Raise the price

effects.log: The treasury fills. The smugglers become heroes. A song about a salt smuggler who outruns the emperor's men is sung in every village. (+800 taels)

choices.text: Lower it, and tax the salt merchants instead

effects.log: The merchants wail. The people salt their soup. Three merchants who wailed loudest turn out to be the smugglers' bankers.

choices.text: Open the salt fields to any licensed seller

effects.log: Chaos for a year, then cheaper salt and a treasury slightly lighter than before. The smugglers have to find honest work.

events.text: It is a jubilee year, and custom says a Son of Heaven may empty the prisons. The Ministry of Justice brings the lists. Thieves, debtors, a poet who insulted a magistrate, and a handful of men who did things that make the minister lower his voice.

choices.text: Free them all. Custom is custom

effects.log: Ten thousand people walk out into the sunlight. Most go home. A few do not, and for a year the magistrates curse your birthday.

choices.text: Free the debtors and the poet only

effects.log: The poet writes you an ode. It is excellent and slightly rude. You have it framed.

choices.text: Read every case yourself first

effects.log: It takes three months. Your birthday is long past. The right people go free, and the wrong ones stay. It is worth it.

events.text: Murim masters walk the streets of your capital with swords on their backs, settle their feuds in your markets and drink in your wine shops until the furniture breaks. The Prefect of the Capital asks for an edict: no blades inside the walls, for anyone, whatever their sect.

choices.text: Issue the edict

effects.log: The masters grumble and leave their swords at the gate. Within a month they have discovered that fans and pipes can be weapons too.

choices.text: Refuse. The murim built this empire too

effects.log: The swords stay. So do the feuds. The Prefect resigns and is replaced by someone who carries a sword himself.

choices.text: Ban duels in the markets only

effects.log: The duels move to the river bank, where nobody owns the furniture. The market traders are very grateful.

events.text: The Yellow River has broken its dikes in the night. Three prefectures are under water. Refugees are walking towards the capital on every road, carrying their children and their ancestors' tablets. The Minister of Works has been awake for four days and has no voice left.

choices.text: Go to the breach yourself

ok.log: The Son of Heaven in the mud at the breach, carrying sandbags. The dike is closed in nine days. The refugees go home singing.

fail.log: The current takes your feet and the guards pull you out. You stay anyway, wrapped in a blanket, giving orders. (-12 health)

choices.text: Open every granary on the road (1000 taels)

effects.log: Rice on every road. Nobody starves who reaches it. The treasury will feel it for years. (-1000 taels)

choices.text: Order the army to dig a new channel

effects.log: Twenty thousand soldiers turn into diggers. The river goes where it is told. Three villages downstream did not agree to receive it.

events.text: The beacons along the northern wall are lit, one after another, all the way to the capital. The steppe has come south in force: twenty thousand horsemen under a young khan who has never lost. The generals argue. The ministers argue. Everyone turns to the throne.

choices.text: Lead the army north yourself

ok.log: Three months on the frontier. The young khan loses for the first time, to you. He sends you a horse with his compliments.

fail.log: A hard campaign and an arrow in the thigh. The khan withdraws in autumn, undefeated. The court says nothing. (-15 health)

choices.text: Hold the wall and wait for winter

effects.log: The khan's horses cannot eat stone. By the first snow the steppe goes home. The villages outside the wall are not so lucky.

choices.text: Send silk and silver to buy peace (800 taels)

effects.log: The khan takes the silk and goes home. He will be back. Everyone knows it. For now the beacons are dark. (-800 taels)

events.text: General Wei has won again. Three campaigns, three victories, and the soldiers of the north sing his name before yours. He has asked for nothing. He sends you every captured banner. Your ministers say that a general who asks for nothing is the most dangerous general of all.

choices.text: Recall him with honours to a desk in the capital

effects.log: General Wei comes home, bows, and sits at a desk for years, very loyally, and very sadly.

choices.text: Trust him and give him more

effects.log: He goes on winning. He never marches south. Some generals are what they look like. You hope this is one of them.

choices.text: Invite him to dinner alone, with no guards

effects.log: Two old soldiers, one table, no guards. He talks about his mother's dumplings all night. He is loyal. Probably.

events.text: The great khan of the steppe sends an envoy with a hundred horses and a request: a bride from the imperial house, to bind your two peoples. The envoy bows correctly and waits. Every minister has an opinion, and none of them will have to ride north and live in a tent.

choices.text: Send a willing kinswoman with a great escort

effects.log: A cousin who wants to see the steppe, and who rides better than the envoy. Twenty years of peace, and a khan's son who speaks your language.

choices.text: Refuse politely, with gifts (400 taels)

effects.log: Silk, tea, jade. The khan takes the gifts and the refusal. His envoy says, smiling, that he will ask again. (-400 taels)

choices.text: Invite the khan to send a son to study here

effects.log: The khan's third son arrives in spring, homesick and curious. He goes home in a few years, half one people and half the other.

events.text: The tribute caravan from the steppe arrives: horses, furs, falcons, and a pair of camels that nobody asked for. In return custom demands gifts worth twice as much. The Minister of Revenue has calculated that the empire loses money on every horse. The Minister of War says the horses are worth it.

choices.text: Give the customary double gifts (300 taels)

effects.log: The tribute is received with ceremony. The steppe is pleased, and its horses carry your cavalry for years. (-300 taels)

choices.text: Keep only the horses and send back the camels

effects.log: The camels are returned with a polite note. The khan finds this very funny. Relations have never been warmer.

choices.text: Set up a horse market at the frontier instead

effects.log: Trade, not tribute. Both sides grumble about the prices. Both sides profit. The frontier is quieter than it has been in a century. (+200 taels)

events.text: The Martial Alliance sends its elders to the throne with a petition bound in blue silk. They ask that the murim be judged by its own laws, by its own elders, and that no magistrate may arrest a master of a sect. The magistrates have sent a petition of their own. It is much longer.

choices.text: Grant it. The murim judges its own

effects.log: The elders bow to the floor. The magistrates bow less. Within a year, every bandit in the land claims to belong to a sect.

choices.text: Refuse. One law under Heaven

effects.log: The elders leave stiffly. The Alliance does not rebel. It does stop sending you birthday gifts.

choices.text: A joint court of elders and magistrates

ok.log: The first session ends in a brawl. The tenth ends in a verdict. By the hundredth, both sides grudgingly respect each other.

fail.log: Neither side will sit with the other. The joint court meets once, in two separate rooms, and is quietly forgotten.

events.text: An envoy of the Demonic Cult arrives at the palace openly, in black and crimson, carrying a gift of a jade chessboard. The Cult asks for nothing, the envoy says, except that the throne does not take sides in the murim's quarrels. The palace guards have their hands on their swords and the envoy finds this charming.

choices.text: Accept the chessboard and the terms

effects.log: The Cult keeps out of your provinces and your court, mostly. The orthodox sects call you a coward in letters they do not sign.

choices.text: Have the envoy thrown out

effects.log: The envoy leaves laughing. Within a month, three tax caravans vanish on the western roads. The Cult has replied.

choices.text: Play a game with the envoy on the board

ok.log: You win by two stones. The envoy bows lower than before. The Cult, apparently, respects that.

fail.log: You lose by half a stone. The envoy is gracious about it, which is worse. The board stays on your desk.

events.text: An envoy in black and crimson comes from the Cult that raised you. The Heavenly Demon sends congratulations and a reminder: the throne was climbed by a disciple of the Cult, and the Cult would like the western provinces to forget the word heresy. The envoy smiles as if this were a small thing.

choices.text: Grant the Cult its western peace

effects.log: The western provinces stop hunting the Cult. The orthodox sects stop trusting the throne. Both were expected.

choices.text: "The throne owes no sect anything."

effects.log: The envoy stops smiling. The Cult does not forget, but it does not move either. For now you are the larger beast.

choices.text: Offer the Cult a seat in the Board of Rites

effects.log: A Cult elder in court robes, arguing about the colour of sacrificial silk. It is the strangest year the Board has ever had.

events.text: Midnight in the inner palace. Your lamp gutters. Three figures in black are crossing the roof tiles of the Hall of Mental Cultivation with the soft step of people who have done this before. The guards are at the far gate. The bell rope is across the room.

choices.text: Meet them on the roof

ok.log: Three assassins on the roof tiles, then none. The guards arrive to find the Son of Heaven sitting on the ridge, catching breath.

fail.deathCause: assassins on the roof of the inner palace
fail.log: A poisoned blade opens your arm before you drive them off. The physicians work until dawn. (-25 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell and bar the doors

effects.log: The bell. The doors. The guards. Two assassins are taken alive and say nothing for a week, and then everything.

choices.text: Blow out the lamp and wait in the dark

effects.log: They search an empty room by moonlight. You are in the rafters. When they leave, you follow them to the house that sent them.

events.text: Your food taster, a quiet old eunuch who has tasted every dish you have eaten since the coronation, puts down his chopsticks halfway through the plum chicken and sits very still. Then he smiles, apologises for the delay, and says the chicken is a little over-salted. His hands are shaking.

choices.text: Call the physicians for him at once

ok.log: Your own qi and the physicians' needles. He lives. The cook is found to have a new house and no explanation.

fail.log: He dies before dawn, still apologising about the salt. You have him buried like a minister.

choices.text: Find the cook before anyone else does

effects.log: The cook is caught at the north gate in a laundry cart. He names a name. It is a name you expected.

choices.text: Eat nothing for a week but rice you cooked yourself

effects.log: The Son of Heaven at a brazier, cooking rice. The court is appalled. You are alive. The rice is terrible.

events.text: The old Chancellor Bai, who has served three emperors and argued with all of them, asks to retire. He is eighty-one. He has told you you were wrong to your face on two hundred and eleven occasions; he has kept a count. On about half of them, you have since admitted, he was right.

choices.text: Refuse. You still need someone to be wrong in front of

effects.log: He grumbles and stays. The count reaches three hundred. He dies at his desk, mid-argument, which is how he would have wanted it.

choices.text: Let him go with every honour

effects.log: A house by the lake, a pension, a title. He writes you a letter every month telling you what you are doing wrong. (-200 taels)

choices.text: Ask him to choose his successor

effects.log: He chooses a young censor nobody likes. Within a year you understand why. The count begins again at one.

events.text: The Minister of Revenue opens the doors of the Inner Treasury for you. Echoes. Dust. A few chests of silver at the back that look lonely. Wars, floods, a palace roof, and thirty years of officials who were very good at arithmetic in the wrong direction.

choices.text: Audit every ministry

ok.log: Three hundred officials investigated. Forty dismissed. A great deal of silver discovered under a great many floors. (+1000 taels)

fail.log: The officials close ranks. You recover a little and earn a great many enemies. (+300 taels)

choices.text: Melt down the palace's gold ornaments

effects.log: Golden cranes, golden lamps, a golden chamber pot that nobody admits ordering. The treasury breathes again. (+600 taels)

choices.text: Raise the land tax

effects.log: The vaults fill. The villages empty a little. Somewhere a magistrate is already adding a fee of his own. (+800 taels)

events.text: The Minister of Revenue proposes a solution to the treasury: sell minor offices. Assistant sub-prefect, deputy inspector of granaries, keeper of the imperial ducks. Rich merchants' sons will pay handsomely, he says, and the ducks will hardly notice.

choices.text: Sell them

effects.log: The treasury fills fast. Within five years the granaries are kept by men who cannot count grain. The ducks are fine. (+1200 taels)

choices.text: Refuse, and tax the merchants' luxuries

effects.log: Silk, pearls, imported wine. The rich complain and pay. The offices go to people who passed the examination. (+400 taels)

choices.text: Sell titles, not offices

effects.log: A merchant can be an Honorary Gentleman of the Ninth Rank with a hat to prove it. He cannot run a granary. Everyone is happy. (+800 taels)

events.text: The palace examination, the final one, is set by the throne itself. Three hundred candidates kneel in the great hall with brushes ready. Each of them has studied for twenty years. One question from you will decide which of them governs the empire for the next forty.

choices.text: "How should a ruler be corrected?"

effects.log: The best answer comes from a farmer's son who says: by honest men, often, without fear. You make him a censor.

choices.text: "What does a hungry village need first?"

effects.log: Rice, says half the hall. Roads, says one candidate, so the rice can reach it. You make that one a prefect.

choices.text: 'Describe this hall's roof without looking up.'

effects.log: Most of them panic. Three describe it perfectly. They notice things. You will need people who notice things.

events.text: The Crown Prince, {npc}, is reading the dynastic histories in the library and has reached the chapter on how the last dynasty fell. {He} has been on the same page for three days. The tutors report that {he} has asked them seven times whether it could happen again.

choices.text: Read the chapter with {npc}

effects.log: You read it together, slowly. {npc} asks good questions. You do not have good answers to all of them. You say so.

choices.text: Tell {npc} it cannot happen to this dynasty

effects.log: {npc} nods, and believes you, and you feel uneasy all evening. Every dynasty believed that.

choices.text: Send {npc} to live a year in a village

effects.log: A year of rice planting and village quarrels. {npc} comes home sunburnt, quieter, and much better at history.

events.text: For the first time the Crown Prince, {npc}, stands in the morning audience and speaks against a minister: the grain tax of Jiangnan is unjust, and here are the numbers. {His} voice cracks once. The numbers are right. The minister turns to the throne with the face of a man who expects to be protected.

choices.text: Back {npc} before the court

effects.log: The minister bows. {npc} goes red to the ears and stands taller for the rest of the audience. The court starts paying attention.

choices.text: Say nothing and let {npc} fight it alone

effects.log: {npc} wins, barely, by stubbornness and numbers. Afterwards {he} asks why you were silent. "Because you did not need me."

choices.text: Rebuke {npc} for speaking out of turn

effects.log: {npc} kneels and apologises. The minister smirks. The grain tax stays. You lie awake wondering who you were protecting.

events.text: The Crown Prince, {npc}, kneels and asks to be sent to the northern frontier with the army. Every dynasty that lasted, {he} says, had heirs who knew the smell of a camp. Every dynasty that ended early, your ministers whisper, lost its heir to a stray arrow.
events.arc: The Crown Prince Asks for a Sword

choices.text: Send {npc} north, with your best general

effects.log: Two years on the frontier. {npc} comes back with a scar, a horse, and soldiers who would die for {him}. Worth the sleepless nights.

choices.text: Refuse. The heir is too precious

effects.log: {npc} obeys. The soldiers never meet their next emperor. One day that will matter, though not today.

choices.text: Spar with {npc} first

ok.log: You win, barely. {npc} goes north with your blessing and a bruise on {his} shoulder that {he} is very proud of.

fail.log: {npc} wins. You are older than you thought. {npc} goes north, and you start training again in the mornings.

events.text: {npc}, your child, has been at court for a year now and is learning its rules faster than you would like. Today a minister you dislike gave {him} a fine horse. {npc} accepted it with a perfect bow and an expression you recognise, because you have worn it yourself.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the horse cost

effects.log: "A favour, later." {npc} says it as if it were obvious. It is obvious. You are proud and frightened in equal parts.

choices.text: Have the horse returned

effects.log: {npc} sulks for a month. The minister understands the message. So, eventually, does {npc}.

choices.text: Let {npc} keep it and learn the price

effects.log: The favour is called in a year later. {npc} pays it, winces, and never accepts a horse again.

events.text: {npc}, your child, comes to you at night with a pack on {his} back. Not a throne, {he} says. Not a court. A mountain, a sect and a sword, like the heroes in the storybooks. {He} is asking permission, which is the only reason {he} is still here.

choices.text: Give {npc} a good sword and your blessing

effects.log: {npc} goes out by the side gate before dawn. The court is scandalised. You sleep better than you have in years.

choices.text: Forbid it. Blood has duties

effects.log: {npc} unpacks. {He} serves well, and is never quite happy, and never quite forgives you.

choices.text: Say yes, after ten years at court

effects.log: A bargain. {npc} counts the days. When the ten years are up, {he} goes anyway, and has learned more than {he} expected.

events.text: The court painters present your official portrait. You are three feet taller than in life, seated on a throne of clouds, with a halo of dragons and a face so serene it could be anyone's. The painters wait, trembling, to learn whether they have been too modest.

choices.text: Order a second portrait, true to life

effects.log: The second portrait has your crooked tooth and the scar. The court hangs the first. You keep the second in your study.

choices.text: Accept it. A dynasty needs its myth

effects.log: The portrait hangs in the ancestral temple. In two hundred years scholars will argue about the dragons.

choices.text: Ask them to paint the court instead

effects.log: A scroll forty feet long: ministers, eunuchs, cooks, the cat. You are a small figure in one corner. It becomes a national treasure.

events.text: The court historian refuses to show you what has been written about your reign, which is his right by a law older than any dynasty. You could change the law. Your grandfather's grandfather's historian was put to death for refusing, and his younger brother took the brush and wrote the same line.

choices.text: Respect the law and never ask again

effects.log: The historian bows deeply. Whatever is written about you, it is true. Some nights that is a comfort.

choices.text: Ask what one line would be

effects.log: He thinks, and then says: "It would say you asked." You laugh. He does not.

choices.text: Command him to show you

effects.log: He hands you the scroll and resigns. The new historian writes, first of all, that you demanded to see the old one's work.

events.text: No rain for a hundred days. The rice is yellow in the fields. The people say Heaven has turned its face from the throne, and they say it in the capital's markets, loudly, under the palace walls. The Board of Rites proposes that the Son of Heaven pray for rain on foot, bareheaded, in the sun.

choices.text: Walk to the altar bareheaded

effects.log: Ten miles in the sun, the whole capital following. It rains three days later. Nobody can prove it was you. Nobody tries.

choices.text: Dig wells, not prayers

effects.log: Two thousand wells in a summer. Half the rice is saved. The Board of Rites is offended. The farmers are not. (-300 taels)

choices.text: Blame the Minister of Rites and dismiss him

effects.log: A minister falls. No rain does. The people notice which of the two you could arrange.

events.text: A peasant army has risen in the south under a leader called the Lord of Yellow Heaven. They wear yellow cloths on their heads and say that your dynasty's time is over. You remember, quite clearly, how dynasties fall: this way, a season at a time.

choices.text: Crush them at once

ok.log: The rising is broken in a season. The yellow cloths are buried. The reasons they were worn are not.

fail.log: The rising slips away into the hills, stronger for surviving. The south now sings its songs.

choices.text: Send rice and an amnesty

effects.log: Half the army goes home with rice in its sacks. The Lord of Yellow Heaven is left with a few hundred and a hat. (-500 taels)

choices.text: Meet their leader under a truce

effects.log: A tired schoolteacher with a list of grievances, all true. You fix six of them. He goes home. Not everyone in his army does.

events.text: A phoenix has been seen over the southern mountains, say forty reports from forty prefects, each describing it slightly differently. The court is ecstatic. The Board of Rites wants a festival. Your oldest minister wants to know why the prefects all reported it in the same week as the tax assessment.

choices.text: Declare a festival of thanks

effects.log: Lanterns, music and phoenix-shaped cakes. Nobody sees the phoenix again. Nobody minds. (-300 taels)

choices.text: Send an inspector to find the bird

effects.log: The inspector finds a golden pheasant, a lot of hopeful prefects and three who were hiding tax arrears. Useful bird.

choices.text: Say Heaven needs no bird to speak

effects.log: The court is disappointed. The people repeat the line in tea houses for years. It becomes a proverb.

events.text: The engineers unroll a map the length of the throne hall: a canal from the southern rice lands to the capital, eight hundred miles long. It will feed the north for a thousand years. It will cost more than the treasury holds, and a hundred thousand labourers will dig it.

choices.text: Begin it (1000 taels)

effects.log: The first spade goes in on the first day of spring. A thousand years is a long time to wait for gratitude. (-1000 taels)

choices.text: Begin it with paid labour only (1500 taels)

effects.log: Paid labour costs more and digs slower and nobody dies of the whip. The engineers think you are mad. (-1500 taels)

choices.text: Mend the old roads instead

effects.log: No canal. Good roads. The south feeds the north slowly and safely. History will never mention you for it.

events.text: Years in. The canal has reached the Huai and stopped there, in a marsh where the fever takes a labourer a day. The overseers want more men. The labourers' families want them home. A petition with ten thousand thumbprints is brought to the palace gate.

choices.text: Halt the work until the fever season ends

effects.log: The canal waits. The labourers go home for the summer. The marsh does not care, but the families do.

choices.text: Send physicians and pay double (600 taels)

effects.log: Physicians, mosquito nets, better rice. The fever kills fewer. The canal moves on. (-600 taels)

choices.text: Press on. The canal must be finished
