effects.log: The canal crosses the marsh by autumn. The marsh is full of graves. The thumbprint petition is kept in the archives.

events.text: The canal is finished. The first rice barges come up from the south on a spring morning, a line of sails as far as the eye can see, and the people of the capital line the banks to watch. An old labourer with a bent back is standing at the front of the crowd, crying.

choices.text: Ride the first barge into the capital

effects.log: The Son of Heaven on a rice barge. The crowd roars. The rice is unloaded by nightfall. The north will not go hungry this century.

choices.text: Find the old labourer and walk with him

effects.log: He dug for six years. He lost a brother in the marsh. He shows you the stretch he dug. You remember it for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Carve the labourers' names on the lock gates

effects.log: A hundred thousand names, cut into stone over four years. Some are misspelt. People come to touch them anyway.

events.text: Your new Chancellor, {npc}, is the most capable official you have ever met. The treasury is full for the first time in years. The roads are mended. The reports are all excellent. {He} smiles very easily, and every official who has criticised {him} has been posted somewhere warm and far away.

choices.text: Praise {npc} and give {him} a free hand

effects.log: The treasury grows. So does {npc}'s household. You tell yourself one is the price of the other. (+500 taels)

choices.text: Set a censor to watch {npc} quietly

effects.log: The censor reports in a month. Nothing wrong. Too nothing. You leave the censor in place.

choices.text: Recall one of the officials sent far away

effects.log: The official comes back thin and sunburnt and asks to speak to you alone. {npc} sends you a basket of very fine peaches.

events.text: A letter in {npc}'s own hand, intercepted at a border post on its way to a prince of the old dynasty who lives in exile. It talks about the weather, and about how a tree with rotten roots falls in the first storm, and about the date of the spring sacrifice, when the palace guard will be thin.

choices.text: Arrest {npc} tonight

effects.log: Soldiers at {npc}'s gate at midnight. {He} is found dressed and waiting, as if expecting company.

choices.text: Change the guard, and say nothing

effects.log: The spring sacrifice comes and the guard is doubled, quietly. Nothing happens. {npc} watches you very carefully all day.

choices.text: Show {npc} the letter, privately

effects.log: {npc} reads it, folds it, and hands it back. "A forgery," {he} says, "and a good one." Neither of you believes it.

events.text: {npc} kneels before the throne in a plain white robe, without the cap of office. {He} has confessed nothing and denied nothing. The whole court is waiting. Half of them owe their posts to {npc}, and every one of them is trying very hard to look like the other half.

choices.text: Exile {npc} to the far south

effects.log: {npc} goes south with one cart. The court breathes out. Years later you hear {he} runs the best school in Lingnan.

choices.text: Pardon {npc} and keep the talent

effects.log: {npc} serves you for ten more years, perfectly, and never again writes about the weather. You never stop reading {his} mail.

choices.text: Strip {npc} of rank and fortune

effects.log: {npc}'s household is emptied into the treasury. It takes forty carts. {npc} is left a house and a garden. (+1500 taels)

events.text: The Crown Prince, {npc}, comes to you white with anger. A faction at court has been gathering signatures for another of your blood to be named heir instead: younger, quieter, and much easier to steer. The list of names is long. Some of them dined at your table last week.

choices.text: Confirm {npc} as heir before the whole court

effects.log: The edict is read at dawn. The faction goes silent, which is not the same as going away. {npc} stands very straight.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why the faction wants another

effects.log: {npc} says it is ambition. Then, slowly, that some of the complaints may be true. That is the first sign {he} may be ready.

choices.text: Let the factions fight it out

effects.log: A throne is not given; it is held. {npc} looks at you for a long time and goes away to gather signatures of {his} own.

events.text: Years on. The quarrel over the heir has split the court in half. The faction has its own banquets, its own poets and its own palace guard captain. Last night, at the Lantern Festival, {npc}'s carriage was blocked in a street for an hour by a cart that nobody owned.

choices.text: Dismiss the guard captain

effects.log: The captain is sent to guard a granary in the far west. The faction loses its sword. It still has its tongue.

choices.text: Summon both sides to one banquet

effects.log: A very long dinner. Nobody eats. Everybody watches everybody. By dessert, a few of the faction have quietly changed seats.

choices.text: Let the heir handle it alone

effects.log: The heir buys the cart's owner, then the poets, then the banquets. Not the way you would have done it. It works.

events.text: The faction's leader comes to you at last, alone, and kneels. The other candidate never wanted the throne, the leader says, and has written to say so. The faction is finished. {npc}, the Crown Prince, is waiting outside the door to hear what you will do with the leader.

choices.text: Let {npc} decide the faction leader's fate

effects.log: {npc} chooses mercy and a post in a far province. A ruler who can pardon is harder to overthrow. You are relieved.

choices.text: Punish the faction leader yourself

effects.log: Exile, and the faction's estates to the treasury. {npc} watches and learns. You are not sure what {he} learns.

choices.text: Make the faction leader the heir's tutor

effects.log: An enemy turned teacher. {npc} is furious, then curious, then wiser. The court calls it the cleverest thing you ever did.

events.text: Locusts in the west, and then no rain, and now famine. Reports come in from three provinces of people eating bark and selling their children for rice. The governor of Shaanxi writes that he has opened his granaries and they were already empty. Somebody has been selling the empire's rice.

choices.text: Open the capital's granaries (800 taels)

effects.log: Barges of rice go west within the week. The people eat. Now somebody must answer for the empty granaries. (-800 taels)

choices.text: Send an inspector with the imperial sword

effects.log: The inspector rides west with the power of life and death. Officials in three provinces start burning ledgers.

choices.text: Let the provinces manage

effects.log: The provinces cannot. A hundred thousand die. The people of the west will remember the name of your reign.

events.text: The inspector returns with a confession and forty carts of hidden rice. The Governor of the West sold the granaries to grain merchants over ten years. He is your second cousin. Every relative at court is watching what the throne does with its own blood.

choices.text: The law, as for anyone

effects.log: The sentence is carried out. Your relatives stop asking for posts in the provinces. The people of the west light incense.

choices.text: Exile him, and return the rice to the west

effects.log: Family is spared. Rice is returned. The west grumbles that a cousin's neck is worth more than theirs. It is not wrong.

choices.text: Make him pay it all back, tael for tael

effects.log: He sells everything he owns. The money goes to rebuild the west. Your cousin lives in one room now and writes poems about injustice. (+600 taels)

events.text: A broom star hangs over the palace, its tail pointing west. The Bureau of Astronomy has been up for three nights. The chief astronomer kneels, sweating: by every book in the archive, a broom star over the palace means the throne will change hands within the year.

choices.text: Thank the astronomer for honesty

effects.log: He is so surprised he forgets to stand. You ask him to keep watching and to tell you the truth either way.

choices.text: Order the books corrected

effects.log: By morning the books say a broom star means a good harvest. The astronomers know. Soon so does the capital.

choices.text: Go up on the roof and look at it yourself

effects.log: A smear of light and cold stars. Heaven does not seem to be talking to you in particular. It is strangely comforting.

events.text: The broom star has long since faded. You are still on the throne. Since it hung there, three plots were uncovered, two of them real; a governor rebelled and was talked down; and the chief astronomer has aged ten years. He asks, with great dignity, what should be written in the annals.

choices.text: "The throne changed hands: from fear to steadiness."

effects.log: The astronomer writes it down with a straight face. It becomes the most quoted line of your reign.

choices.text: "A comet was seen. Nothing happened."

effects.log: Plain and true. Later astronomers cite it to prove that comets mean nothing. The old books are quietly revised.

choices.text: "Write that the throne was tested and held."

effects.log: The line goes into the annals. The plotters who were not caught read it too, and wait for the next comet.

events.text: The court celebrates the anniversary of your coronation. Some of the ministers who knelt at it are gone. Their sons kneel now, and a few of their grandsons. A young official recites the achievements of your reign, and it takes him most of the morning, and you remember some of them differently.

choices.text: Correct him, kindly, where he is wrong

effects.log: The young official blushes and writes it all down. The annals of your reign become slightly less glorious and much more true.

choices.text: Let him finish. They need the story

effects.log: A reign is partly what happened and partly what is told. You let them tell it. It sounds like a good reign.

choices.text: Remit the year's taxes in thanks (800 taels)

effects.log: The villages celebrate your anniversary with you, for once with full bowls. (-800 taels)

events.text: This morning your hand shook as you set the imperial seal on an edict, and the impression came out blurred. The secretary noticed. The secretary pretended not to notice. By noon, you suspect, half the court knows that the Son of Heaven's hand shook.

choices.text: Seal the next hundred edicts yourself, steady

effects.log: A hundred edicts, a hundred perfect seals, one at a time, all afternoon. The court gets the message. Your wrist does not forgive you.

choices.text: Let the Chancellor share the seal

effects.log: The Chancellor seals edicts beside you now. The court bows to two people. It is the first step down the stairs, and you know it.

choices.text: Circulate your qi and practise every dawn

effects.log: Breath, slow movements, the old forms from your youth. The shake goes. Some of it comes back in winter.

events.text: The Crown Prince, {npc}, is no longer young either. {He} has grey at the temples and has been the heir for a very long time. {He} has never once complained. At dinner {he} pours your tea, and you notice {he} has started to hold the cup the way you do.

choices.text: Give {npc} a province to rule outright

effects.log: {npc} rules it well and comes home every New Year with a report. An heir who has ruled something is half an emperor already.

choices.text: Talk to {npc} about the day you are gone

effects.log: A long night, a jar of wine, everything you know. {npc} listens without interrupting, the way you never could.

choices.text: Say nothing. The throne is still yours

effects.log: {npc} goes on pouring the wine. The court watches the two of you very carefully. So does history.

events.text: The geomancers have chosen a site for your tomb: a south-facing valley in the western hills, with water in front and a mountain behind, where the dragon veins meet. Work could begin this year. Some emperors spent half their reigns building their tombs. Some spent their dynasties.

choices.text: A modest tomb, finished in a year

effects.log: A tomb fit for a prince, not a god. The labourers go home in a year. The people approve. The geomancers sulk.

choices.text: A great tomb, worthy of the dynasty (1000 taels)

effects.log: Halls under the hill, an avenue of stone animals, guardian generals taller than houses. People will visit it for a thousand years. (-1000 taels)

choices.text: No tomb. Scatter the ashes over the river

effects.log: The court is horrified. The Board of Rites faints in sequence. You feel lighter than you have in years.

events.text: In the middle of a long audience about canal tolls you realise you are no longer listening, and have not been for some time. You are thinking about a mountain, and the sound of a waterfall, and a small kitchen with a smoking stove, a life you have never had or have not had for a long time. The ministers are waiting for an answer.

choices.text: Answer them, and keep the thought for later

effects.log: You answer about the canal tolls. The thought stays, folded up inside your sleeve like a letter you have not sent.

choices.text: Ask the oldest minister how one steps down

effects.log: The old man is silent a long time. "Slowly, Your Majesty," he says at last. "And with the door left open behind."

choices.text: Cancel the afternoon and walk in the garden

effects.log: An hour by the pond. A carp comes up to look at you. The canal tolls can wait one day. The empire survives it.

events.text: Against the advice of every physician, you insist on one more inspection tour of the provinces. The court prepares for a procession of a thousand carriages. You would rather take twenty riders and see what the provinces look like when they do not know you are coming.

choices.text: Twenty riders and plain clothes

effects.log: You see the empire as it is: better than you feared in some places, worse in others. Three magistrates are very surprised.

choices.text: The full procession, for the people to see

effects.log: A thousand carriages and banners to the horizon. Villages line the roads. Everyone sees the emperor. Nobody sees the empire. (-400 taels)

choices.text: Stay, and send a trusted prince of the blood instead

effects.log: The prince goes in your place and comes back with a report full of things you did not know. It is time, perhaps, to listen more.

events.text: The first morning after you set down the seal. No drums at dawn. No ministers at the door. Nobody needs an edict, a judgement or a decision on the colour of anything. A sparrow lands on the windowsill and looks at you as if you were simply a person. It is very strange.

choices.text: Sleep until noon

effects.log: You have not slept until noon since you were a child. You wake confused, then delighted. The sparrow is still there.

choices.text: Walk out through the side gate into the city

effects.log: A noodle stall, a crowd, a street performer. Nobody recognises you. You eat two bowls and pay with your own silver.

choices.text: Practise the forms of your youth in the yard

effects.log: Slow, then less slow. Your body remembers more than your court ever let it. The sparrow leaves, unimpressed.

events.text: You have begun writing an account of your reign. Not the annals; your own. The first chapter is about the day you first saw the throne hall. The second chapter has been crossed out four times. A former minister who visits for tea asks, carefully, whether you intend to name names.

choices.text: Name every name, the good and the bad

effects.log: The former minister goes pale and asks for more tea. Word reaches the capital within a week. Several old officials go to the provinces for their health.

choices.text: Write only about the mistakes

effects.log: It is a short book about a long reign, and every page is about something you got wrong. It is the best thing you have written.

choices.text: Burn the second chapter for good

effects.log: Some things are better unwritten. You burn it in the brazier and pour the minister more tea. Neither of you mentions it again.

events.text: The memoir is finished. A scholar asks to copy it. A publisher in Hangzhou offers silver for it. The throne sends a polite letter asking to see it first, which is not a request. You hold the manuscript in your lap and feel the whole reign in its weight.

choices.text: Send it to the throne with your blessing

effects.log: The throne reads it in a night and sends it back with a single line: "Thank you for the mistakes." You keep the letter in the book.

choices.text: Have it printed for anyone to read

effects.log: It sells out in Hangzhou in a week. Students argue about it in every tea house. Some of the arguments are very good. (+200 taels)

choices.text: Seal it in the tomb, to be read in a hundred years

effects.log: Let it be history before it is gossip. The manuscript goes into a stone box. You feel lighter.

events.text: You walk the capital in plain clothes. In a tea house a storyteller is telling the story of your reign, and getting most of it wrong. In his version you killed a tiger with a single blow. The audience is enthralled. The old woman next to you says she always thought you looked taller.

choices.text: Correct the storyteller from the audience

effects.log: He argues with you. The audience takes his side. You lose an argument about your own life and enjoy it enormously.

choices.text: Pay for the next story, about anyone else

effects.log: The storyteller moves on to a fox spirit. You drink your tea and listen with real pleasure. (-5 taels)

choices.text: Laugh, and tell the old woman she is right

effects.log: She pats your arm and says you must have been handsome once. You thank her and mean it.

events.text: The new reign is making a mistake you can see from your garden: a tax on river barges that will strangle the southern trade within three years. You made the same mistake once. Nobody has asked your opinion. Former emperors who give opinions have a way of being moved to more distant gardens.

choices.text: Write a private letter, very carefully

effects.log: Three drafts. The tax is quietly reduced in the spring. Nobody mentions your letter. That is how you know it was read.

choices.text: Say nothing. It is not yours any more

effects.log: The tax strangles the southern trade for three years and is then repealed. The new reign learns, as you did.

choices.text: Invite the Minister of Revenue to tea

effects.log: The minister comes, nervous, and leaves thoughtful. Officially you discussed peonies. The tax is amended in a month.

events.text: Your garden was meant for peonies and rare stones. You have dug up the peonies and planted cabbages, radishes and a stubborn row of beans. The palace gardener who was sent to look after you is in despair. The cabbages, however, are excellent.

choices.text: Send the best cabbages to the throne

effects.log: The throne receives two cabbages with full ceremony and serves them at a state banquet. The cabbage becomes fashionable.

choices.text: Teach the gardener to grow beans

effects.log: The gardener comes round to the beans. By autumn the two of you argue about compost like old soldiers.

choices.text: Plant the peonies back in one corner

effects.log: Peonies and cabbages, side by side. Beauty and supper. It seems the right way to end things.

events.text: An old enemy comes to your gate: a minister you exiled, or a general you defeated, it is hard to remember which now. Bent, white-haired, leaning on a stick. He says he has come to see whether you look as old as he does. He brought a jar of wine to find out.
events.arc: An Old Enemy at the Gate

choices.text: Invite him in and brew the good tea

effects.log: You both look very old. You raise your teacups to it. By midnight you are arguing about the same battle, and enjoying it more than you did then.

choices.text: Apologise for what you did to him

effects.log: He is silent a long time. Then he says he would have done the same, and worse. The wine tastes better after that.

choices.text: Send him away. Some doors stay shut

effects.log: He goes without a word. You stand behind the gate longer than you meant to. The wine he left on the step is excellent.

events.text: Clearing an old chest, you find your first seal: not the imperial one, but a small stone seal from before the throne, from the years when your name meant little to anyone. The stone is chipped. The carving is clumsy. You remember the market stall where you had it cut.

choices.text: Press it once on clean paper

effects.log: Your old name, red on white. It looks very young. You hang it on the wall beside the window.

choices.text: Give it to the youngest of your blood

effects.log: The child looks at it, puzzled. "It is not even jade." "No," you say. "That is the point." Perhaps one day.

choices.text: Keep it in your sleeve from now on

effects.log: A small weight in your sleeve, every day. When people bow too low, you touch it.

events.text: Children in the lane are playing at emperors. One of them is you. The child playing you has a paper crown and a stick for a sword, and is conquering the well. Another child is the last dynasty, and is losing with great dignity. Then they argue over how the story ends, because nobody knows yet.

choices.text: Tell them how it ends

effects.log: You tell them. They listen with great seriousness, then decide your ending is boring and give it a dragon.

choices.text: Watch from the gate and say nothing

effects.log: The child with the paper crown wins, loses, wins again. That is about right. You go back inside smiling.

choices.text: Ask to play the last dynasty

effects.log: You lose with even greater dignity. The children are delighted. Your knees are not. It is the best afternoon of the year.
